A3654BE94FB3441BA43820B695FBCD4D.description: Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to reveal and explain properties of the quantity represented by the expression.

773B53743C55485C8EB73EE57E2A34A9.description: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems

13EA017C975A4D2D856EF3698699D1F6.description: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it.
comments: For example, see x<sup>4</sup> — y<sup>4</sup> as (x²)² — (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² — y²)(x² + y²).
For example, interpret P(1+r)<sup>n</sup> as the product of P and a factor not depending on P.
5965A91480954A0593276A6263F81DAA.description: Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity.

B62F3071EDA34B518453DB1E6551B03D.description: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

BD82AB9197D2457E93D2259782E15EBA.description: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context
comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

2966BA16E86B4229AD47BD099B200FE3.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

98833658F55142AFB09BDF36455EE82B.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

A636F33EB5174286BDDFEB62E0F000A5.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
AB45D1305B9942659E11DC8DFEB97749.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

711C5C9E10364BA2AEB3665EBA4867B2.description: Count to tell the number of objects.

E50F46226B304EF2814AD022A2391F5F.description: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

08C4DF70D31C4E7795499E6C53F76C4C.description: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

F9276452981045F3BFF45E51B009446F.description: Know number names and the count sequence.

document.title: K-12 Mathematics New Hampshire Curriculum Framework

BB750890DFE60131766368A86D17958E.description:
Students will recognize, explore, and develop mathematical connections and be able to:
  • Link conceptual and procedural knowledge (e.g., they will know that when they "regroup," they are simply changing the representation of the minuend, but not its value).
  • Recognize and use mathematics in other curriculum areas (e.g., science, social studies).
  • Recognize and use mathematics in their daily lives (e.g., graphs, tables, or maps).
  • Identify mathematical situations occurring in literature for children.
  • Identify examples of geometry in nature, art, and architecture.

BB74C2A0DFE60131766268A86D17958E.description:
Students will create and use representations to communicate mathematical ideas and to solve problems and be able to:
  • Create and use age level appropriate representations to organize, record, and communicate mathematical ideas (e.g., students should recognize the relationship among seven counters, seven tally marks, and the symbol 7).
  • Select, apply, and translate among mathematical representations to solve problems (e.g., representing fractions with circles, with geoboards, and with pattern blocks).
  • Link different representations.
  • Use representations to model and interpret physical, social, and mathematical phenomena.
  • Use conventional and self-generated (invented) representations and connect them.
  • Realize that any representation is subject to multiple interpretations (e.g., drawings and graphs can be read in a different way).

BB747DF0DFE60131766168A86D17958E.description:
Students will communicate their understanding of mathematics and be able to:
  • Demonstrate mathematical communication through discussion, reading, writing, listening, and responding, individually and in groups.
  • Discuss relationships between everyday language and mathematical language and symbols (e.g., words that mean something different in mathematics and in everyday life).
  • Explain conclusions, thought processes, and strategies in problem-solving situations.
  • Discuss, illustrate, and write about mathematical concepts and relationships.
  • Draw pictures and use objects to illustrate mathematical concepts.

BB73BAB0DFE60131765F68A86D17958E.description:
Students will use mathematical reasoning and proof and be able to:
  • Use models, known facts, properties, and relationships to explain their thinking.
  • Justify solution processes and answers (e.g., "I chose this method to solve the problem because…").
  • Draw conclusions using inductive reasoning.
  • Identify the missing information needed to find a solution to a given story problem.
  • Use patterns and relationships to analyze mathematical situations (e.g., count by fives).

BB736F00DFE60131765E68A86D17958E.description:
Students will use problem-solving strategies to investigate and understand increasingly complex mathematical content and be able to:
  • Formulate and solve multi-step problems from everyday and mathematical situations.
  • Solve problems using a variety of strategies (e.g., working backwards, looking for patterns and relationships; guess and check; making tables, charts, or organized lists; solving a simpler version of a problem, drawing a diagram; or creating a model)
  • Verify and interpret results with respect to the original problem.
  • Determine if the solution of a problem is reasonable.
  • Solve problems using manipulatives, graphs, charts, diagrams, and calculators.
  • Demonstrate that a problem may be solved in more than one way.
  • Exhibit confidence in their ability to solve problems independently and in groups.
  • Display increasing perseverance, and persistence in problem solving.

BB72F8D0DFE60131765C68A86D17958E.description: Analyzes patterns, trends, or distributions in data in a variety of contexts by determining or using more, less, or equal (e.g., Have there been more, less, or the same number of cloudy days compared to sunny days this week?).

BB72BCC0DFE60131765B68A86D17958E.description: Interprets a given representation created by the class (models and tally charts) to answer questions related to the data, or to analyze the data to formulate conclusions using words, diagrams, or verbal/scribed responses to express answers.

BB7234F0DFE60131765968A86D17958E.description: Identifies and extends to specific cases a variety of patterns (sequences of shapes, sounds, movement, colors, and letters) by extending the pattern to the next one, two or three elements, or by translating AB patterns across formats (e.g., an abb pattern can be represented as snap, clap, clap or red, yellow, yellow) or by identifying number patterns in the environment.

BB71B2D0DFE60131765768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates understanding of spatial relationships using location and position by using positional words to locate and describe where an object is found in the environment.

BB7175D0DFE60131765668A86D17958E.description: Determines elapsed and accrued time as it relates to calendar patterns (days of the week, yesterday, today, and tomorrow), the sequence of events in a day; and identifies a clock and calendar as measurement tools (days of week, months of the year).

BB713580DFE60131765568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates conceptual understanding of measurable attributes using comparative language to describe and compare attributes of objects (length [longer, shorter], height [taller, shorter], weight [heavier, lighter], temperature [warmer, cooler], and capacity [more, less]); and compares objects visually and with direct comparison.

BB70F470DFE60131765468A86D17958E.description: Uses properties, attributes, composition, or decomposition to sort or classify polygons (triangles, squares, rectangles, rhombi, trapezoids, and hexagons) or objects by using one non-measurable or measurable attribute; and recognizes, names, and builds polygons and circles in the environment.

BB706910DFE60131765268A86D17958E.description: Makes estimates of the number of objects in a set (up to 20) by making and revising estimates as objects are counted (e.g., A student estimates the number of pennies in a jar as 20. Then the student counts the first 10 and makes another estimate based on those that have been counted and those that remain in the jar.).

BB6FFD80DFE60131765168A86D17958E.description: Mentally adds and subtracts whole numbers by naming the number that is one more or one less than the original number.

BB6FB500DFE60131765068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates understanding of monetary value through investigation involving knowing the names and values for coins (penny, nickel and dime).

BB6F6B60DFE60131764F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates conceptual understanding of mathematical operations through investigations involving addition and subtraction of whole numbers (from 0 to 10) by solving problems involving joining actions, separating actions, part-part whole relationships, and comparison situations; and addition of multiple one-digit whole numbers.

BB6F2290DFE60131764E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates understanding of the relative magnitude of numbers from 0 to 20 through investigations that demonstrate one-toone correspondence; that compare whole numbers to each other or to benchmark whole numbers (5, 10); that demonstrate an understanding of the relation of inequality when comparing whole numbers by using "1 more" or "1 less"; that connect numbers orally and written as numerals to the quantities that they represent using models, representations, or number lines.

BB6EDFA0DFE60131764D68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates conceptual understanding of rational numbers with respect to: whole numbers from 0 to 12 through investigations that apply the concepts of equivalency in composing or decomposing numbers using models, explanations, or other representations; and positive fractional numbers (1/2) as "fair share" (i.e., equal sized parts or sets) using models, explanations, or other representations.

document.title: K-12 Reading New Hampshire Curriculum Framework

B12489C0DFE6013163A568A86D17958E.description: Participating in discussions about text, ideas, and student writing by offering comments and supporting evidence, recommending books and other materials, and responding to the comments and recommendations of peers, librarians, teachers, and others (Local)

B1243FA0DFE6013163A468A86D17958E.description: Self-selecting reading materials aligned with reading ability and personal interests (Local)

B123EDF0DFE6013163A368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates participation in a literate community by…

B1239C30DFE6013163A268A86D17958E.description: Reading from a wide range of genres/kinds of text and a variety of authors (e.g., literary, informational, and practical texts) (Local)

B1234980DFE6013163A168A86D17958E.description: Reading with frequency, including in school, out-of-school, and summer reading (Local)

B122E7E0DFE6013163A068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates the habit of reading widely and extensively by…

B121F730DFE60131639D68A86D17958E.description: Using strategies while reading or listening to literary and informational text. (Local)
comments: of reading comprehension strategies might include: using prior knowledge; predicting and making text-based inferences; determining importance; generating literal and clarifying questions; constructing sensory images (e.g., making pictures in one's mind); making connections (text to self, text to text, and text to world); or locating and using text features (e.g. headings, parts of the book) (See also Appendix D)

B121B5D0DFE60131639C68A86D17958E.description: Uses comprehension strategies (with flexibility and as needed)…

B1217300DFE60131639B68A86D17958E.description: Using a range of self-monitoring and self-correction approaches (e.g., predicting upcoming text, monitoring, adjusting and confirming, through use of print, syntax/language structure, semantics/meaning, or other context cues [e.g., pictures], etc.) (Local)

B1212E40DFE60131639A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates ability to monitor comprehension for different types of texts and purposes by…

B120E4F0DFE60131639968A86D17958E.description: Strategies for Monitoring and Adjusting and Reading Comprehension Strategies (RS:1), (RS:2)

B12047B0DFE60131639768A86D17958E.description: Making inferences about causes or effects, when signal words are present (State)
comments: "The sun came out. Then the puddle dried up. What made the puddle dry up?"

B11FBA00DFE60131639568A86D17958E.description: Making basic inferences or drawing basic conclusions (State)
comments: "Based on this report, do turtles make good pets?"

B11F70D0DFE60131639468A86D17958E.description: Recognizing generalizations about text (e.g., identifying appropriate titles or main/central ideas) (State)

comments: Combining or comparing facts and details presented – "What food is eaten by both kinds of fish?"

B11ED300DFE60131639268A86D17958E.description: Analyze and interpret informational text, citing evidence as appropriate by…

B11E84B0DFE60131639168A86D17958E.description: Analysis and Interpretation of Informational Text (Expository and Practical Text across Content Areas) / Citing Evidence (IT:2)

B11E3720DFE60131639068A86D17958E.description: Distinguishing among a variety of types of text (e.g., reference: beginning dictionaries, glossaries, children's magazines, content trade books, children's newspapers; and practical/functional/texts: procedures/instructions, announcements, book orders, invitations) (Local)

B11DE6C0DFE60131638F68A86D17958E.description: Generating questions before, during, and after reading to enhance recall, expand understanding and/or gain new information (Local)

B11DA140DFE60131638E68A86D17958E.description: Locating and recording information to show understanding, when given an organizational format (e.g., T-chart or Venn diagram) (Local)

B11D5480DFE60131638D68A86D17958E.description: Using explicitly stated information to answer questions (State)
comments: "According to this report, what do dolphins eat?"

B11CFF30DFE60131638C68A86D17958E.description: Obtaining information, from text features (e.g., simple table of contents, glossary, charts, graphs, diagrams, or illustrations) (State)
comments: "On what page would you find information about snakes?"

B11CB690DFE60131638B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate initial understanding of informational texts (expository and practical texts) by…

B11C7510DFE60131638A68A86D17958E.description: Initial Understanding of Informational Text (Expository and Practical Text across Content Areas) (IT:1)

B11BEE40DFE60131638868A86D17958E.description: Comparing stories or other texts to related personal experience, prior knowledge, or to other texts (Local)

B11BA2E0DFE60131638768A86D17958E.description: Generates a personal response to what is read through a variety of means by…

B11B54C0DFE60131638668A86D17958E.description: Recognizing explicitly stated causes or effects (Local)

B11B0FF0DFE60131638568A86D17958E.description: Identifying possible motives of main characters (Local)
comments: "Why did the wolf want to blow the house down?"

B11A8AA0DFE60131638368A86D17958E.description: Making basic inferences about problem or solution (State)
comments: "What helped Luke to solve his problem in the story?" "What was Jane's problem?"

B11A45B0DFE60131638268A86D17958E.description: Identifying relevant physical characteristics or personality traits of main characters (State)

comments: What might happen next?

B11997D0DFE60131638068A86D17958E.description: Analyze and interpret elements of literary texts, citing evidence where appropriate by…

B1194850DFE60131637F68A86D17958E.description: Analysis and Interpretation of Literary Text, Citing Evidence (LT:2), (LT:3), (LT:4)

B118E420DFE60131637E68A86D17958E.description: Identifying literary devices as appropriate to genre: rhyme, repeated language or dialogue (e.g., "When I was young in the mountains…" ) (Local)

B118A230DFE60131637D68A86D17958E.description: Distinguishing among a variety of types of text (e.g., literary texts: poetry, plays, realistic fiction, fairy tales, fables, tall tales, or fantasy) (Local)

B1185F70DFE60131637C68A86D17958E.description: Generating questions before, during, and after reading to enhance recall, expand understanding and/or gain new information (Local)

B11805D0DFE60131637B68A86D17958E.description: Retelling the key elements of a story (Local)

B117BBE0DFE60131637A68A86D17958E.description: Sequencing key events in order, as appropriate to text (Local)

B1176D40DFE60131637968A86D17958E.description: Identifying or describing character(s), setting, problem, solution, or major events, as appropriate to text (State)

B1170120DFE60131637868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate initial understanding of elements of literary texts by…

B1160DB0DFE60131637568A86D17958E.description: Selecting appropriate words to use in context, including words specific to the content of the text (State)
comments: In a short passage about Native American homes, students might encounter the words longhouse and igloo, and then be asked to show that they know the difference between them.

B115CB60DFE60131637468A86D17958E.description: Identifying synonyms or antonyms; or categorizing words (State)
comments: (of categorizing): Given a T-chart with two "categories" of words listed (e.g., shapes and sizes), students would identify another word to add to the chart that describes shapes or sizes; or in a multiple choice item, select the best category title for the words listed

B11589A0DFE60131637368A86D17958E.description: Shows breadth of vocabulary knowledge, demonstrating understanding of word meanings or relationships by…

B1150370DFE60131637168A86D17958E.description: Using strategies to unlock meaning (e.g., knowledge of word structure, including common base words and suffixes, such as "thickest," "hopeful;" or context clues, including illustrations and diagrams; or prior knowledge) (State)

B114B8B0DFE60131637068A86D17958E.description: Students identify the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary by…

B113C120DFE60131636D68A86D17958E.description: Reading grade-appropriate, highfrequency words (including irregularly spelled words) (Local)

B1137DD0DFE60131636C68A86D17958E.description: Reading grade-level appropriate words (in connected text) with automaticity (Local)

B1133B00DFE60131636B68A86D17958E.description: Reading regularly spelled one or two syllable words using knowledge of sounds and letter patterns (Local)

B112F4E0DFE60131636A68A86D17958E.description: Identifying regularly spelled multi syllabic words, by using knowledge of sounds, syllable types, or word patterns (including most common spellings for consonants and vowels, e.g., knot, catch, float, fight; or common suffixes (State)
comments: Students might be asked to match words to pictures or to match words to words with similar sounds (e.g., flower and shower)
(multi syllabic words): happiness, shower, sunshine

B112A3C0DFE60131636968A86D17958E.description: Applies word identification and decoding strategies by…

B111B4C0DFE60131636668A86D17958E.description: Fluency: reading grade-appropriate text in a way that makes meaning clear, demonstrating phrasing, expression, and with attention to punctuation (including commas and quotation marks) (Local)

B1111640DFE60131636568A86D17958E.description: Fluency: reading grade-appropriate text with oral fluency rates of at least 80-100 words correct per minute (Local)

B110D470DFE60131636468A86D17958E.description: Accuracy: reading material appropriate for the end of grade 2 with at least 90-94% accuracy (Local)

B10FCF40DFE60131636068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating 1-1 matching of words spoken to words in print (Local)

B10F7CF0DFE60131635F68A86D17958E.description: Identifying basic punctuation marks and their usage (e.g., question marks, periods, quotation marks) (Local)

B10EF120DFE60131635D68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates understanding of concepts of print during shared or individual reading by…

B10DE280DFE60131635968A86D17958E.description: Deleting phonemes in one-syllable words ("What is "crust" without the 'c'?") (Local)

B10D9500DFE60131635868A86D17958E.description: Isolating phonemes in single syllable words (e.g., "Tell me the first sound in 'mop';" "Tell me the last sound in 'mop,'" "Tell me the middle sound in 'mop.'") (Local)

B10D5380DFE60131635768A86D17958E.description: Blending and segmenting phonemes in one syllable words (e.g., f-i-sh, r-u-n) (Local)

B10D1080DFE60131635668A86D17958E.description: Blending and segmenting phonemes in more complex one-syllable words (which may include combinations of blends and digraphs, as in th-i-ck, t-r-a-sh) (Local)

document.title: K-12 Science Literacy New Hampshire Curriculum Framework

B661DF00DFE601316D7068A86D17958E.description: Understand that some scientific jobs/careers involve the application of physical science content knowledge and experience in specific ways that meet the goals of the job.

B66124E0DFE601316D6E68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between durable goods, which are designed to operate for a long period of time, and non-durable goods, which are only intended to operate for a short period of time.

B660D110DFE601316D6D68A86D17958E.description: Describe how natural resources, such as coal, oil and natural gas are tapped for use in power plants, and how alternative sources, such as solar, wind, water, nuclear are tapped for power; and compare the advantages and disadvantages of each source.

B6607610DFE601316D6C68A86D17958E.description: Explain how humans use natural resources, such as flowing water and burning of coal, oil, or natural gas to generate electrical energy in power plants.

B6601D40DFE601316D6B68A86D17958E.description: Social Issues (Local and Global) Energy, Power, and Transportation Manufacturing

B65FBBE0DFE601316D6A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate appropriate use of tools, such as rulers, calculators, balances, and graduated cylinders to measure and calculate volume and mass.

B65EFE90DFE601316D6868A86D17958E.description: Understand that design features, such as size shape, weight, and function, must be considered when designing new technology.

B65E3DD0DFE601316D6668A86D17958E.description: The growth of scientific knowledge in Physical Science has been advanced through the development of technology and is used (alone or in combination with other sciences) to identify, understand and solve local and global issues.

B65DD8C0DFE601316D6568A86D17958E.description: Explain how the motion of an object can be described by its position, direction of motion, and speed; and illustrate how that motion can be measured and represented graphically.

B65D7F40DFE601316D6468A86D17958E.description: Explain that an object in motion that is unaffected by a force will continue to move at a constant speed and in a straight line.

B65CCBE0DFE601316D6268A86D17958E.description: Use data to determine or predict the overall (net) effect of multiple forces (e.g., friction, gravitational, magnetic) on the position, speed, and direction of motion of objects.

B65C7260DFE601316D6168A86D17958E.description: Recognize the general concepts related to gravitational force.

B65C0D00DFE601316D6068A86D17958E.description: Explain that the force of gravity gets stronger the closer one gets to an object and decreases the further away one gets from it.

B65B6690DFE601316D5E68A86D17958E.description: The motion of an object is affected by force.

B65B0C60DFE601316D5D68A86D17958E.description: Use data to draw conclusions about how heat can be transferred (convection, conduction, radiation).

B65AAF30DFE601316D5C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that most chemical and nuclear reactions involve a transfer of energy.

B65A4970DFE601316D5B68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the human eye can only detect wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation within a narrow range; and explain that the differences of wavelength within that range of visible light are perceived as differences in color.

B659C9F0DFE601316D5A68A86D17958E.description: Describe ways light can interact with matter, such as transmission (which includes refraction), absorption, and scattering (which includes reflection).

B6595600DFE601316D5968A86D17958E.description: Recognize the Sun is a major energy source for the Earth, and describes how it affects the planet's surface.

B65902D0DFE601316D5868A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between kinetic energy, which is the energy of motion and potential energy, which depends on relative position.

B6584900DFE601316D5668A86D17958E.description: Collect data or use data provided to infer or predict that the total amount of mass in a closed system stays the same, regardless of how substances interact (conservation of matter).

B657EC50DFE601316D5568A86D17958E.description: Explain the law of conservation of energy.

B6572950DFE601316D5368A86D17958E.description: Given a real-world example, show that within a system, energy transforms from one form to another (i.e., chemical, heat, electrical, gravitational, light, sound, mechanical).

B656CF20DFE601316D5268A86D17958E.description: Explain that states of matter depend on the arrangement of the molecules and their motion.

B6566F50DFE601316D5168A86D17958E.description: Explain that oxidation involves combining oxygen with another substance, as in burning or rusting.

B6561C70DFE601316D5068A86D17958E.description: Identify factors that affect reaction rates, such as temperature, concentration and surface area; and explain that dissolving substances in liquids often accelerates reaction rates.

B655C840DFE601316D4F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how substances react chemically with other substances to form new substances, known as compounds, and that in such recombinations, the properties of the new substances may be very different from those of the old.

B6551400DFE601316D4D68A86D17958E.description: Energy is necessary for change to occur in matter. Energy can be stored, transferred and transformed, but cannot be destroyed.

B654AB40DFE601316D4C68A86D17958E.description: Represent or explain the relationship between or among energy, molecular motion, temperature, and states of matter.

B6544BF0DFE601316D4B68A86D17958E.description: Given data about characteristic properties of matter (e.g., melting and boiling points, density, solubility), identify, compare, or classify different substances.

B653F960DFE601316D4A68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the relationships among mass, volume and density.

B653A6A0DFE601316D4968A86D17958E.description: Identify a molecule as the smallest part of a substance that retains its properties.

B6534F50DFE601316D4868A86D17958E.description: Explain how different substances of equal volume usually have different weights.

B652F160DFE601316D4768A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between volume and mass and define density.

B6524260DFE601316D4568A86D17958E.description: Given graphic or written information, classify matter as atom/molecule or element/compound (not the structure of an atom).

B651E2B0DFE601316D4468A86D17958E.description: Collect data or use data provided to infer or predict that the total amount of mass in a closed system stays the same, regardless of how substances interact (conservation of matter).

B6516AE0DFE601316D4368A86D17958E.description: Identify methods used to separate mixtures, such as boiling, filtering, chromatography and screening.

B65106E0DFE601316D4268A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between a mixture and a pure substance.

B650AC30DFE601316D4168A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between an atom and an molecule.

B65054C0DFE601316D4068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that elements can combine in a variety of ways to form compounds.

B64FEDC0DFE601316D3F68A86D17958E.description: Explain that atoms often combine to form a molecule or formula unit (crystal).

B64F2950DFE601316D3D68A86D17958E.description: All living and nonliving things are composed of matter having characteristic properties that distinguish one substance from another (independent of size/amount of substance).

B64E8040DFE601316D3B68A86D17958E.description: Understand that some scientific jobs/careers involve the application of life science content knowledge and experience in specific ways that meet the goals of the job.

B64DD020DFE601316D3968A86D17958E.description: Describes ways biotechnology helps humans, including improved health and medicine.

B64D6720DFE601316D3868A86D17958E.description: Give examples of how increased understanding of biology has led to improvements in biotechnology, such as scientific methods for increasing the yield or the pestresistance of important food crops.

B64D0930DFE601316D3768A86D17958E.description: Explain the necessity of and purpose for the proper disposal of medical products.

B64CA790DFE601316D3668A86D17958E.description: Social Issues (Local And Global) Medical Technology and Biotechnology

B64C4F20DFE601316D3568A86D17958E.description: Recognize and provide examples of how technology has enhanced the study of life sciences, as in the development of advanced diagnosing equipment improving medicine.

B64B8130DFE601316D3368A86D17958E.description: Provide examples of ways technology is used to protect the environment, such as using bacteria to clean water.

B64B28C0DFE601316D3268A86D17958E.description: Explain how technology has influenced the course of history, and provide examples such as those that relate to agriculture, sanitation and medicine.

B64A8140DFE601316D3068A86D17958E.description: The growth of scientific knowledge in Life Science has been advanced through the development of technology and is used (alone or in combination with other sciences) to identify, understand and solve local and global issues.

B64A2BB0DFE601316D2F68A86D17958E.description: Using data provided, select evidence that supports the concept that genetic information is passed on from both parents to offspring.

B649D440DFE601316D2E68A86D17958E.description: Describe the major changes that occur over time in human development from single cell through embryonic development to new born (i.e., group of cells during the first trimester, organs form during the second, organs mature during the third).

B6497370DFE601316D2D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that an organism can be described in terms of a combination of traits; and differentiate between inherited traits and those that result from interactions with the environment.

B64917B0DFE601316D2C68A86D17958E.description: Compare patterns of human development with those of other vertebrates.

B6484F30DFE601316D2A68A86D17958E.description: Use data and observations to support the concept that environmental or biological factors affect human body systems (biotic and abiotic).

B647E9C0DFE601316D2968A86D17958E.description: Describe the function of white blood cells and explain how they support the body's defense system.

B6477760DFE601316D2868A86D17958E.description: Describe how viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites may affect the human body and provide examples of how they can interfere with normal body function.

B6472040DFE601316D2768A86D17958E.description: Recognize that disease in organisms can be caused by intrinsic failures of the system or infection from other organisms.

B6464F00DFE601316D2568A86D17958E.description: Explain how all behavior is affected by both inheritance and experience.

B645E600DFE601316D2468A86D17958E.description: Explain that organism's behavioral response is a reaction to internal or and environmental stimuli, and that these responses may be determined by heredity or from past experience.

B6459270DFE601316D2368A86D17958E.description: Recognize that unlike human beings, behavior in insects and many other species is determined almost entirely by biological inheritance.

B644E3B0DFE601316D2168A86D17958E.description: Humans are similar to other species in many ways, and yet are unique among Earth's life forms.

B63EE230DFE601316D1168A86D17958E.description: Cite examples supporting the concept that certain traits of organisms may provide a survival advantage in a specific environment and therefore, an increased likelihood to produce offspring.

B63E8330DFE601316D1068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that humans are able to control some characteristics of plants and animals through selective breeding; and explain how this results in small differences between the parents and offspring, which can accumulate in successive generations so that decedents are very different from their ancestors.

B63E20D0DFE601316D0F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how individual organisms with certain traits are more likely than others to survive and have offspring.

B63DC030DFE601316D0E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in any given environment the growth and survival of organisms depend on the physical conditions that exist; and explain that in all environments, organisms with similar needs may compete with one another for resources, including food, space, water, air, and shelter.

B63D5D90DFE601316D0D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that hereditary information is contained in genes, which are located in the chromosomes of each cell; and explain that inherited traits can be determined by either one or many genes, and that a single gene can influence more than one trait, such as eye and hair color.

B63CA200DFE601316D0B68A86D17958E.description: Use a model, classification system, or dichotomous key to illustrate, compare, or interpret possible relationships among groups of organisms (e.g., internal and external structures, anatomical features).

B63C4940DFE601316D0A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the concept of extinction and describes its importance in biological evolution.

B63BF170DFE601316D0968A86D17958E.description: Describe how the fossil record provides geologic evidence verifying the existence of now extinct life forms, and explains how this evidence provides documented proof of their appearance, diversification and extinction.

B63B0800DFE601316D0768A86D17958E.description: Describe the type of impact certain environmental changes, including deforestation, invasive species, increased erosion, and pollution containing toxic substances, could have on local environments.

B63A4B30DFE601316D0568A86D17958E.description: Groups of organisms show evidence of change over time (e.g. evolution, natural selection, structures, behaviors, and biochemistry).

B64486C0DFE601316D2068A86D17958E.description: Given an ecosystem, trace how matter cycles among and between organisms and the physical environment (includes water, oxygen, food web, decomposition and recycling, but not carbon cycle nor nitrogen cycle).

B6441EE0DFE601316D1F68A86D17958E.description: Identify carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus as common elements of living matter.

B643C8C0DFE601316D1E68A86D17958E.description: Describe how matter is recycled within ecosystems and explain that the total amount of matter remains the same, though its form and location change.

B6436EF0DFE601316D1D68A86D17958E.description: Know that all organisms, including humans, are part of, and depend on, two main interconnected global food webs: one which includes microscopic ocean plants, and the other which includes land plants.

B6430B00DFE601316D1C68A86D17958E.description: Explain the process of respiration and differentiate between it and photosynthesis.

B642A8F0DFE601316D1B68A86D17958E.description: Identify autotrophs as producers who may use photosynthesis, and describe this as the basis of the food web.

B641DC60DFE601316D1968A86D17958E.description: Given a scenario, trace the flow of energy through an ecosystem, beginning with the sun, through organisms in the food web, and into the environment (includes photosynthesis and respiration).

B64180E0DFE601316D1868A86D17958E.description: Explain how food provides energy and materials for growth and repair of body parts.

B640A2A0DFE601316D1668A86D17958E.description: Using data and observations, predict outcomes when abiotic/biotic factors are changed in an ecosystem.

B64042E0DFE601316D1568A86D17958E.description: Explain that in all environments, organisms with similar needs may compete with one another for resources, including food, space, water, air, and shelter, and that in any particular environment the growth and survival of organisms depend on the physical conditions.

B63FEA60DFE601316D1468A86D17958E.description: Explain how changes in environmental conditions can affect the survival of individual organisms and an entire species.

B63F3880DFE601316D1268A86D17958E.description: Energy flows and matter recycles through an ecosystem.

B639F690DFE601316D0468A86D17958E.description: Using data provided, select evidence that supports the concept that genetic information is passed on from both parents to offspring.

B6399EB0DFE601316D0368A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast sexual reproduction with asexual reproduction.

B6393FB0DFE601316D0268A86D17958E.description: Explain how the basic tissues of an embryo form.

B638D4D0DFE601316D0168A86D17958E.description: Explain that the fertilized egg cell, carrying genetic information from each parent, multiplies to form the complete organism.

B6386FD0DFE601316D0068A86D17958E.description: Explain that in sexual reproduction, a single specialized cell from a female merges with a specialized cell from a male in a process called fertilization.

B6381270DFE601316CFF68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a species of sexually reproducing organisms is comprised of all the organisms that can mate to produce fertile offspring.

B637BFB0DFE601316CFE68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction, and explain that in some kinds of organisms, all the genes come from one parent, while in organisms requiring two sexes to reproduce, typically half the genes come from each parent.

B6370F80DFE601316CFC68A86D17958E.description: Using data and observations about the biodiversity of an ecosystem, make predictions or draw conclusions about how the diversity contributes to the stability of the ecosystem.

B636BA80DFE601316CFB68A86D17958E.description: Explain relationships between or among the structure and function of the cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems in an organism.

B6366520DFE601316CFA68A86D17958E.description: Explain why it is beneficial for an organism to be able to regulate its internal environment while living in a constantly changing external environment.

B6360E60DFE601316CF968A86D17958E.description: Define a population and describe the factors that can affect it.

B635A3A0DFE601316CF868A86D17958E.description: Identify the functions of the human body's systems, including digestion, respiration, reproduction, circulation, excretion, movement, control and coordination and protection from disease; and describe how they interact with one another.

B634CA50DFE601316CF668A86D17958E.description: Describe or compare how different organisms have mechanisms that work in a coordinated way to obtain energy, grow, move, respond, provide defense, enable reproduction, or maintain internal balance (e.g., cells, tissues, organs and systems).

B6347910DFE601316CF568A86D17958E.description: Recognize that similarities among organisms are found in anatomical features and patterns of development; and explain how these can be used to infer the degree of relatedness among organisms.

B633D190DFE601316CF368A86D17958E.description: All living organisms have identifiable structures and characteristics that allow for survival (organisms, populations, and species).

B6330A20DFE601316CF168A86D17958E.description: Understand that some scientific jobs/careers involve the application of Earth Space science content knowledge and experience in specific ways that meet the goals of the job.

B6325980DFE601316CEF68A86D17958E.description: Identify the potential impact of converting forested land to uses such as farms, homes, factories, or tourist attractions.

B6320160DFE601316CEE68A86D17958E.description: Explain how technologies can reduce the environmental impact of natural disasters.

B6319650DFE601316CED68A86D17958E.description: Explain how to test natural materials to measure and compare their properties.

B6312790DFE601316CEC68A86D17958E.description: Provide examples of how creative thinking and economic need has shaped the way people use natural materials, such as the use of metal ores, petroleum, and fresh water.

B6306000DFE601316CEA68A86D17958E.description: Describe how man uses land-based light telescopes, radio telescopes, satellites, manned exploration, probes and robots to collect data.

B62ED130DFE601316CE668A86D17958E.description: Recognize the importance of technology as it relates to science, for purposes such as: access to space and other remote locations, sample collection and treatment, measurement, data collection, and storage, computation, and communication of information.

B62E7D80DFE601316CE568A86D17958E.description: Describe ways in which technology has increased our understanding of the world in which we live.

B62DD2E0DFE601316CE368A86D17958E.description: The growth of scientific knowledge in Earth Space Science has been advanced through the development of technology and is used (alone or in combination with other sciences) to identify, understand and solve local and global issues.

B62D7340DFE601316CE268A86D17958E.description: Describe the universe as being comprised of billions of galaxies, each containing many billions of stars; and explain that there are vast distances separating these galaxies and stars from one another and from the Earth.

B62CC7D0DFE601316CE068A86D17958E.description: Describe objects such as asteroids, comets and meteors in terms of their characteristics and movement patterns.

B62C0770DFE601316CDE68A86D17958E.description: Explain that special units of measure, such as light years and astronomical units, are used to calculate distances in space.

B62BA0A0DFE601316CDD68A86D17958E.description: Define an astronomical unit as the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

B62AF7F0DFE601316CDB68A86D17958E.description: The origin and evolution of galaxies and the universe demonstrate fundamental principles of physical science across vast distances and time.

B62AA240DFE601316CDA68A86D17958E.description: Explain how technological advances have allowed scientists to re-evaluate or extend existing ideas about the Solar System.

B628A790DFE601316CD568A86D17958E.description: Explain the effects of gravitational force on the planets and their moons.

B6284060DFE601316CD468A86D17958E.description: Identify the characteristics and movement patterns of the planets in our Solar System and differentiate between them.

B6230EF0DFE601316CC568A86D17958E.description: Explain how sediments of sand and smaller particles, which may contain the remains of organisms, are gradually buried and cemented together by dissolved minerals to form solid rock.

B622BD20DFE601316CC468A86D17958E.description: Explain that sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic rocks contain evidence of the minerals, temperatures, and forces that created them.

B6226880DFE601316CC368A86D17958E.description: Describe the processes of the rock cycle.

B621B880DFE601316CC168A86D17958E.description: Explain the role of differential heating or convection in ocean currents, winds, weather and weather patterns, atmosphere, or climate.

B6215AD0DFE601316CC068A86D17958E.description: Explain how Earth events, abruptly and over time, can bring about changes on Earth's surface (e.g., landforms, ocean floor, rock features, climate).

B62104E0DFE601316CBF68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the Earth's crust is divided into plates which move at extremely slow rates in response to movements in the mantle.

B6205480DFE601316CBD68A86D17958E.description: Describe how catastrophic changes that have taken place on the Earth's surface can be revealed by satellite images.

B61F9760DFE601316CBB68A86D17958E.description: Explain how fossils found in sedimentary rock can be used to support the theories of Earth's evolution over geologic time; and describe how the folding, breaking, and uplifting of the layers affects the evidence.

B61EC890DFE601316CB968A86D17958E.description: Use geological evidence provided to support the idea that Earth's crust/lithosphere is composed of plates that move.

B61E4CF0DFE601316CB868A86D17958E.description: Describe the layers of the Earth, including the core, mantle, lithosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere.

B61D89D0DFE601316CB668A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe the impact certain factors have on the Earth's climate, including changes in the oceans' temperature, changes in the composition of the atmosphere, and geological shifts due to events such as volcanic eruptions and glacial movements.

B616B390DFE601316CA368A86D17958E.description: Use evidence collected from observations or other sources and use them to create models and explanations.

B6165CF0DFE601316CA268A86D17958E.description: Formulate a scientific question about phenomena, a problem, or an issue and using a broad range of tools and techniques; and plan and conduct an inquiry to address the question.

B607D270DFE601316C7A68A86D17958E.description: Know that different models can be used to represent the same thing; what kind of model is used and how complex it should be depends on its purpose; and the usefulness of a model is one of the instances in which intuition and creativity come into play in science, mathematics and engineering.
