Eighteen Months
: Show interest in other children

3FE4CE26FE3A4A8BB7DB6E63E67D3F06.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Demonstrate increasing
awareness of other children
(E.g. While lying on a blanket
close to her, Carlos reaches
for Becca’s arm.)

7710966B7E6C44AA9102B856505047F3.description:
Relationships and
social skills with
peers

B5F14C4A83884982896F8B68ADEACA87.description:
Three Years: May initiate contact with
unfamiliar adults, when
familiar adults are nearby

9B0C153435394691B7012856D101EC3C.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Are more comfortable around
unfamiliar adults

749B9EF3628A40DFBE6797F9D5848742.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Dependent on experience, may
show more interest in unfamiliar
adults, but are still cautious

4AA76FD7437A4D93B6EF83399500788C.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Continue to show hesitation
around unfamiliar adults (E.g.
Billie hides behind his father
when the store clerk says “hi”
to him.)

9BD052C3A64C4A12BAFFF04DEA77361C.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show strong preference
for familiar adults and may
demonstrate fear or rejection
responses to unfamiliar adults

CC3063269BB947ED94C00B8920B46D5F.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Are able, over time, to
differentiate between familiar
and unfamiliar adults

5F3A82974C5C4DEB80D842834106FB47.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Imitate familiar adults in culturally appropriate ways in everyday situations

F286B65AC81143B19BA9D0D1C70B9CDF.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Seek adult help when needed for emotional support, physical assistance, social
interaction, and approval

4D1F09D83CF648FD934AE3820693936E.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Interact easily with familiar adults, but may be hesitant to approach or respond
to less familiar adults

EF7AE53519634ED99331BFD5E1F29486.description:
Three Years: Respond appropriately to
social and emotional cues of
adults

57BE756F2E7F4974A41551241B51EB88.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Continue to need adult approval
and validation but show more
competence

2A09855AF3BE4DA5829CE42864EE1B61.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Imitate and attempt to please
familiar adults (E.g. Rylee joins
in singing when her caregiver
sings a silly song with her.)

2FACD498E1674BBABC596AEE013BCB4C.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Continue to need the security of
a trusted adult; ask for help, if
needed, in verbal and non-verbal
ways

1357E6CA3D014E4F82F854E722821F18.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Rely on trusted adults to feel
secure trying new activities

2EBCF5C876B04B47A1840A0DC067E5B9.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Demonstrate interest in
familiar adults and develop
strong attachment to primary
caregivers

69E6D86488CF4D3EAE41A736C8D38A8A.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Express or describe their own characteristics and preferences (E.g. Jacob only
chooses brown sweatpants when clothes shopping with his mother.)

D37A2139FA48476995D58F6CF3E396E8.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Notice differences and make comparisons between their physical characteristics
and others’ and the way things are done in different settings (E.g. Consuela
says “My abuela talks Spanish and my grandma talks English.”)

441603C8EF5646BE83ADADB708D83E98.description:
Three Years: Continue to develop
awareness of differences and
their own gender and cultural
identity (E.g. Delia says to her
teacher, “I’m a girl, so I can
be a mommy someday.”)

D32139AC00D14733B14ACB1EBA516601.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Identify or point to characters
that resemble themselves or
their family members in books
or magazines

8C00FBC854034D33A913E16A5E0EF3A6.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Point out or comment on
differences in gender and
physical characteristics, using
social labels (E.g. Eddie points
to each classmate and labels
each as “boy” or “girl.”)

5944E89CE6D04AB88FECB896367F76E6.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Mimic adult behavior and
responses to other people

508C377FC544478E9D3958641CC8BCE6.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show preference for their family
members and primary caregivers

29CAACFBE5904F968C8B10718F5D56D3.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: By 9 months, recognize that
they are separate and distinct
from primary caregivers (E.g.
8-month-old Taniesha cries
whenever her mother leaves
the room.)

14CD5370412C48B49A1635E14E2083A5.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Are confident, self-directed, purposeful and inventive in play

166C581750A94EAC8CBF39470B6105D7.description:
Three Years: Begin to experiment with
their own potential and show
confidence in their own
abilities

B7BDD45DD07A4CF8BD8BAD8CA86598B4.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Show independence and
competence

1F465E9B46404F008C5A0558254E1E8D.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Perform the tasks requested
of them and may initiate tasks
on their own (E.g. Kyle’s nana
spoons food onto his plate
and Kyle says, “Me do it!” and
reaches for the spoon.)

56AF442CEAC145708216E841BA04EDC8.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Show more awareness of their
abilities

CE1379689A1D4B5FBEF8FE8F66E1BE9E.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Take actions in the expectation
of getting a response from
an adult (E.g. 11-monthold Carolyn lifts her arms up
knowing that her caregiver will
pick her up.)

02ED29E5816B457CA458985434DDC4C1.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Smile and laugh when
imitating an adult
(E.g. 8-month-old Ashton
smiles when he imitates his
teacher clapping.)

8DB2956310DB4BCCBB8A88AF19BB8A32.description:
Boast about what they know and can do (E.g. Quinn says, “I am really good at
drawing rainbows.”)

9D12D8CD249A47FC8757392C78A4CACD.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Continue to seek adult attention and recognition of what they know and can do

D281B85A11EA4BDAAF5986F5034A008C.description:
Three Years: Draw adult’s attention to their
actions and creations (E.g. On
the playground Luna keeps
telling her father, “Watch me,
watch me!”)

E692886842B1483CA5D2FAC325B3A2A9.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Call attention to themselves in
photographs or videos

2078E03058804C5F8EE263F130F2B126.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show delight in their abilities

6127116EBA104E238AD91949F3293B5F.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Show awareness of being seen
by others such as repeating
an action when someone is
watching (E.g. Whenever she
sees a camera, Ruby smiles and
poses.)

DF6E6A16FDB94A07BAE9F9F64426F3FD.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show likes and dislikes in ways
that are consistent with the
family’s cultural expectations
(E.g. Brady vocalizes pleasure
while playing, but cries while
having a diaper changed.)

033D1C64B8824BD59EA4556AA12CFCDE.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Smile or are comforted when
a trusted caregiver speaks
kindly to them

standardSets.title: Language Development and Emergent Literacy: Birth-5
standardSets.subject: Early Learning Standards (2016-)

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

D690F644CBD74B3EAB08F000BAECDE92.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Begin to copy or write their own name

6FA4782BB11442F68F0EECCF5A898820.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Engage in writing using letter-like symbols to make letters or words

6C6120DBE40F49D2BB4E281436B9375A.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use scribbles, shapes, pictures, or dictation to represent thoughts or ideas

FD39468ACED04DB7879F633799A0CD9F.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Understand that writing is a way of communicating

445CB9170C9748649D5527076ACCA011.description:
Three Years: Begin to differentiate between
drawing and writing, and their
scribbles may look more like
writing (E.g. After painting
a picture, 3-year-old Isaiah
makes a series of vertical
lines, representing his name.)

1E30013C269F4A6E849BFB94EC1DA2D6.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Use their increased fine motor
control to control the size and
shape of their scribbles

0768CA7B3E2E48B2916C5CCC1A103DB8.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Scribble and draw and see
these as the same

EABB9522DC3346CE8B472F9A2C7584FF.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Gain more control over the kinds
of marks they make (lines vs.
circular marks)

92685F7B71C149B7BCE0DCBB91F439DB.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Use writing tools (crayons,
markers, pens) and notice that
they can make marks with these
utensils

BC49E9A5D5524EC99EFD248CA7F021C3.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Note: Children at this age are
not aware of writing.

66E50ED6430F4C769662FC23BE76B334.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Understand that specific symbols are used to communicate in writing

808D07E1FDBD469D98616E2B75CD29D9.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to associate sounds with words or letters

5D4D929CADF146299E28F6FDC92B0FDF.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Recognize some letters in the alphabet, especially those in their own name
(E.g. While putting her things away in her cubby, 4-year-old Azlyn notices other
children’s names on their cubbies. She exclaims,“Hey, Autumn starts the same
as me!”)

1F44D9DB1CC64AEF8A4BB75EA4E78F4F.description:
Three Years: Begin to recognize their own
name and may notice words
that start with the same letter
as their own name

F0EB3AA61B224416B75582AB3E7AF368.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Point to print and ask, “What
does that say?” or ask
someone to write for them

11E757CC8FF845F29671513F90675D4E.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Recognize that print and
numerals are symbols that
convey meaning (E.g. Colin, age
2, points to the bottom of his
painting on his classroom wall
and says, “There’s my name.”)

DE8FE0D6515F46269770AA2F9726881A.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can show awareness of and
recognize some print in the
environment

6CBC0CC9109948878F4C6FFB4CEE9561.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May begin to recognize that
labels convey meaning (E.g.
Jared sees a box of cheerios
and says, “Oh, Oh!”)

929BF30AF2EA4578A8D88DEDE602F5CB.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Note: Children at this age are
not aware of print as being
distinct from anything else in
their environment.

BFAED2C31E43444989665D12011C4888.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Understand that print carries a message

54B08BFE6A6B4825924B1AC2EDD254D0.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Identify parts of books such as cover, first page, and title

8C1B8021CDD64174A9607E2704649095.description:
Three Years: Understand proper handling of
books to avoid damage and
help repair books, with adult
support

5F2EDBF0FE474F27856C9B128E0389C5.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Can turn the book to the first
page for an adult to begin
reading and close the book and
say, “The end”

B4CA15A0053B435EB7E1E13A462EEF42.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Can identify the front of the book
and use clues on the cover to
select a book (E.g. Using the
cover of the book as a clue,
Charna, 28 months, picks up
The Itsy Bitsy Spider and says to
her mother, “Spider book.”)

279FB439154B4ABB8E0A7A9E78D2D047.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Hold the book properly and
turn pages, sometimes several
at a time

711FDBC6ECD54A04924042333D02A10A.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Look at pictures in books, but
often treat books like other toys
and objects in the environment

A6E57F483F2848BB871B9E3227DB5FCC.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Treat books as any other object
by exploring with hands and
mouth (E.g. 5- month-old Colby
grabs a board book and puts it
to his mouth to chew on it.)

FA375148188142278B091A4AB5A6300F.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Can distinguish the beginning sounds of some words

BE9DC6E6C862455F860E477FFBD0D3DA.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Play with sounds of spoken language including letter sounds, rhymes, and words
(E.g. Ray says, “My name rhymes with play.”)

1C405AF63DFA40409B281ADF243E7FC0.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Listen to and recognize different sounds in rhymes, songs, and familiar words
(E.g. When the teacher sings, “Willaby wallaby Wecca an elephant sat on...”,
Becca shouts, “Becca!”)

7B5D101E855E46D5BBA1873A15115A18.description:
Three Years: Enjoy playing with the sounds
of language (E.g. Claire
laughs loudly when her friend
calls her Clairey Berry.)

059F35F1D94D47BB8CA201C03B6EC7C2.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Participate in chants and songs
and books that rhyme

ECF65E3E70DC48DB91B3CD459B7C5B75.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Enjoy chants and songs and
books that rhyme

C4DE4DFB72CB4F959614216161817218.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Enjoy chants and songs and
books that rhyme

63299A24932440A796673F700EDB3395.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Recognize and react to the
sounds of language and can
discriminate between nonspeech environmental sounds
(E.g. Jamie continues playing
when he hears the refrigerator
door open, but stops when he
hears a jar being opened.)

1E773C6B39824AF79320DB6A4EF81FC2.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Respond to sounds and words
heard often

E60933D242F8427CA73E674D66CFB612.description:
Phonological
awareness
(which refers to
understanding the
sound structure
of language
such as sounds,
rhymes, syllables,
and words)*

96C50F9F7D2C41D19C321DAF6CEEA0FC.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Request or respond to informational books on favorite topics

C1D41E05D605497D9A92ED28E98AB312.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Select favorite books, authors, or illustrators

7DBFBAFD25024CCAB879D053DBAB4334.description:
Three Years: Say what they like about a
favorite book

A7A95A66BD694ACCAFB4AA5C7F3CA762.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Ask for familiar books to be
read in exactly the same way
each time and know when
sections are being skipped

D5A9AADDF6744EC784BFA9EFFAEA2760.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May ask an adult to read the
same book repeatedly

C608552A197947D3BB1813065833617F.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Name and/or ask for favorite
book and may show preference
for books on certain topics

0BC2E29613D4400F9470369B6BADBEA9.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Bring a book to an adult to be
read to and/or respond positively
to an adult’s offer to read

AF5023C1140F4F9FB0F3D284A431EEFD.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Show enjoyment at being
read to through vocalizing,
eye contact, and movement
(E.g. 8-month-old Sophia
squeals in delight when
her mother reads Ten Little
Fingers and Ten Little Toes.)

1A502B0E9B64429A8FE3EDEDC17C0407.description:
Interest in and
appreciation of
reading*

294AC1C709E34C02B43D256700F66C97.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Retell information from a book (E.g. 5 year old Mac tells his Papa that
Tyrannosaurus Rex runs as fast as a horse.)

2778C42A379F420D97E68B6524B49C72.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use their own words to retell a simple familiar story while looking at a book

4EC5A49B379C41848589AFDBD81A2FD3.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Represent stories told or read aloud through a variety of media or in play

75404329175D45C49949E896A6B2422D.description:
Three Years: Can ask and answer simple
questions about the story

00F35D1B6A944DEE9E7658532D960C6B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Ask for familiar books to be
read in exactly the same way
each time and know when
sections are being skipped

ED6183B665AF488F9787A8A67D95666A.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Identify with a particular
character or scene (E.g. When
listening to the book, Where’s
My Teddy Said Eddie, Zaviel,
25 months, makes a scared
face, identifying with the little
boy in the woods.)

12D7FEB77A484E87A91855B75769BFEC.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Point to and vocalize about an
illustration or imitate an action
seen in a picture (E.g. 18-
month-old Angelique imitates the
jumping action of the frog when
being read, Jump Frog Jump.)

AFC9588FBE0F42D28D9F7EADD41DEF00.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May focus on certain elements
in the illustrations, but often
skip pages or focus on a
particular page

1BF8BF3C83BB4B64A0E0DDFC0C890C0B.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Enjoy hearing a book
being read and looking at
the pictures, but do not
understand the sequence of
the story

CD2A7C4C60334D719D43D63AD4A11FB5.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Tell their own stories

847C6BBA863D4669AFAD5D8E1E5840A7.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Guess what will happen next in a story using pictures as a guide

79F12EDB09784DF88195BB99F9067082.description:
Three Years: Relate or retell stories with
more parts

A3EF75FD4BE44F33BF0452F8DDFFAE84.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Can react to dramatic elements
of a story and may respond
with predictions when asked,
“What will happen next?”
(E.g. Addison, 33 months, is
able to predict what is hidden
under the flap on a page of a
familiar book.)

8E38B1F15B5A460DB6790564D57237EB.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May relay or retell simple
stories

973B30A067024B62AC16CB6C9FCD8825.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can recognize that a story is
beginning from a clue such as
‘Once upon a time’

16EF9A61065C42A2A0A99CD837852D01.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Participate in book reading
activities (E.g. Brandon, 15
months, makes a shhh sound
and puts his finger on his lips
at the appropriate time when
reading The Napping House.)

5FA1FF9CCF3040EF9AF6925279230FCC.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Look at the face of an adult
describing the sequence of
what will happen next (E.g.
5-month-old Nate stares
intently at his father’s face
when he describes how he will
change Nate’s diaper.)

C0DE9FF97E494BEA9568418A761F296D.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Make connections between a book or story to personal experiences
(E.g. Irena points to a picture of a dog and says, “I have a dog like this,
only bigger and my dog never chews shoes”.)

095E8DF68DC74FBF8B697F680D878255.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Ask questions about a book or story

E0A94D797A5A425486EE80ACC1F150C9.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Respond to adult questions about a book or story

FD7DF5E426BC43BBB8CB69C5823B1BDB.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Ask for a story to be read and respond to stories told or read aloud

34D423CA1F834AE0A74164FEEA0643EB.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Learn new information from books being read to them

52FC60EB46FD4068868AD8FB855DAB00.description:
Three Years: May describe what’s
happening in the pictures
while turning the pages in a
familiar book

B3608036D99648B7BAD92FE323589841.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Enjoy being read to and looking
at books independently; May
say familiar words and phrases
while looking at the appropriate
page (E.g. Kali, 33 months,
sings along to the repetitious
book, Brown Bear, Brown Bear,
as her teacher reads it to her.)

B432C2367FAE4533BF36F82042CC7874.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: While being read to, point to
and comment on illustrations
and repeat or anticipate familiar
words or phrases in the text

4718E6E69D99413AB5E7A56696B3623D.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: May show preferences for
specific books and turn pages at
the appropriate time with adult
assistance

C34853A316EA45EB8208EB24898657F4.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Enjoy being read to and may
seek opportunities to be read to
and to interact with books

AD21EF1F36804179A41D069097D99D69.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Focus on picture books while
an adult is reading to them
(E.g. 6-month-old Alisha
sits on her mother’s lap and
looks and pats her hand on
the book that her mother is
reading.)

8C2C3ABA7B3B4546A2E0070572B24A74.description:
Participation in
language and
literacy activities*

AD79615E61FE4F04B4016F3D11E2E124.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Tell stories with multiple characters and events

D7F646239E63455A923012A62721A8D8.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Ask questions and initiate and respond in conversations with others

52D89275CC1B49EA8EE6847E48D713D0.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use language for a variety of purposes, including communicating information
(E.g. 5-year-old Sean shows his friends his new race car and they ask him
questions about it and tell him stories about theirs.)

15C99B88088E47269DD2C1D6014F42C4.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Speak clearly enough to be understood

0438391446ED43FC84366DFD9678AED8.description:
Three Years: Can relate a simple story
(E.g. When asked about her
day, Rhianna says, “I went
out on the playground and
it was so icy and I fell and
I cried and cried and my
teacher helped me.”)

F3C8A2C6503147318A236D072CEF1CF8.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Use more connecting words,
such as “and” or “then”

919F3534865641529E1D86D859C5EBDB.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use words and some common
rules of speech to express their
ideas and thoughts (E.g. Margie
exclaims, “I climbed up stairs!”)

90560F3117534D01B39E6D89A015B8FC.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Begin to use words to
communicate and may combine
two to three words to form short
phrases or sentences

9460B57EC699498689B849A7DD4A6AA7.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Move from imitating single
words to beginning to use single
words to communicate

F12A5C54640C477C8170A3490FD9D932.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Begin vocalizing using a
variety of sounds (E.g. Stan
uses different types of cries to
communicate different needs.)

E85E96DC1CDE49029B9624BC3229FC4C.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use words and phrases learned through conversations and being read to
(E.g. 4-year-old Hazel says, “The end”, when she finishes her snack.)

A03DDA046DD74A5E9D07F5825474AA0A.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use increasingly complex and varied vocabulary and language

34FCF1439FE64E858A385561ACC222C5.description:
Three Years: Continue to build their
vocabulary including more
descriptive words

4520EB59426E45A586799D1074EFFB53.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Correctly use a growing number
of vocabulary words and show
interest in new words (E.g. Liam
knows that fast, quick, and
speedy mean the same thing.)

F5C300D1410D47E5B0F57617E9F72D7A.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Demonstrate a burst of new
vocabulary words, which they
may or may not use correctly

30BED481447B480CBA719A578E144A52.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Combine two words to express
wants or needs (E.g. As Harper
walks to the car she says, “Car
go.”)

C9AD0864B6ED4DDCA22DF705119423B2.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Produce their first word and
may have a vocabulary of up to
15 words

D786A146DA6243AA80B4509DAAF2F906.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: At this age children are not
communicating with words

95CA2E04E0114D0A936108E3FCEC0E24.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: With adult support, can take turns in conversations and group discussions

F14FF79D981F433C9C3B527CDFC1EA4F.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use language according to rules appropriate for the cultural context (may need
adult help in recognizing appropriate cultural context) (E.g. 4-year-old Savannah
asks her peer, “Can I please have the purple crayon?”)

4E7387A746114662A0A33F1B60EDAFFF.description:
Three Years: Begin to understand the rules
for communication in different
situations (E.g. Charlie
whispers when dad explains
that he needs to use a quiet
voice when visiting grandpa in
the hospital.)

F688A62FCB774914B8DDF1D48DB9D5F9.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Can participate in simple
conversational exchanges,
usually with adults

83CDB18D8A0D4403A6B3644707448ED1.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use language for a variety of
functions

79FFD1EDA4C04B2D9ACB062ED372257B.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Convey a variety of meanings
through simple vocabulary
(E.g. Jeff says “milk,” which
can mean, “I want milk,” “I’m
finished drinking milk,” or “I
spilled my milk.”)

5367F77CD69447EE9441AFBBDA297FAE.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Begin to use single words to
communicate

5EAA943357E8495688957BBCF194FFA9.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Use sounds to get adult
attention and to engage adults

5DD6E4783AC248D28F640FA385BEA253.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Communicate needs, wants, or thoughts using nonverbal gestures, actions, or
expressions (E.g. 5-year-old Devin points to the block area when he is asked
what he wants to do next.)

AC289692D8B241A08D40FD26D43DAD5C.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Understand non-verbal cues

C049F90BAB744D1CBBED995306A6F2D2.description:
Three Years: Notice other children’s body
language and try to interpret it

41775E3AD5D44B6291FC857358953639.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Begin to understand other
children’s nonverbal social cues

803BD196D82041E9A0B5CD040AF679BE.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use gestures to augment what
they are trying to communicate
with words (E.g. Destiny shakes
her head emphatically as she
says, “No, no, no.”)

9FE47C1B7C30439EA7AA5138BB94A208.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Understand others’ nonverbal
symbolic cues such as nodding
for yes or shaking head for no

F2367465B64846AC89D21981F8B8FAA4.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Communicate using consistent
sounds, gestures, and facial
expressions

057EFB575747472DAB28D0ABCE186ACA.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Use various sounds and
movements to communicate

B4A97F3FE440476CA70BF10E9C3DF7D2.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Follow instructions that include a two or three step sequence of actions such as
setting up a game or following a recipe

DA337E8FDB564B90AB4181609FA93814.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Listen with understanding to stories, directions, and conversations

EA09357D6E21495E92A83FEFE80B143F.description:
Three Years: Show awareness of others’
comments or statements that
have to do with them (E.g.
Milo shouts, “Don’t want
to go to the doctor!” after
overhearing his parents talk
about his illness.)

F77D728C46AF4E8C8C456E96EA60D31C.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Respond to simple questions

B4E76B50373240A282B2DCC401D12AE6.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show by their actions that they
understand simple one-step
directions (E.g. When her
teacher says, “Put on your
coat,” Doretta picks up her
coat and puts her hand in the
sleeve.)

DAFF5A6A3BE4461AA4E14B054C1C07A7.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: May show by their actions
understanding of simple
statements (E.g. Blaine sits
down at the table when his
teacher says, “It’s time to eat.”)

97E8F1DC3ECA4350A767BA155D3ADC05.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Demonstrate their understanding
of others’ speech through their
actions, such as responding
physically to simple requests
(E.g. Joshua, 15 months, smiles
when his father says, “Smile at
Daddy.”)

5787F966607F4605873E80B689E17C6A.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Show interest in the speech
of others and prefer familiar
voices

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

CAFBAFD602994BBC80C5F1F438E89776.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to differentiate between yesterday, today, and tomorrow

58B1D2B996A147CF8C5959302E249413.description:
Three Years: Can remember and describe
daily sequence of events

16220743ECB043ABA2BEC54609C8C66C.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Can anticipate what will happen
next in daily routines

19520DA908824205AE08041B91FC3882.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show increased knowledge and
memory for daily routines

5B665AE5F6DC4F35BD5454E0ACAAD434.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can recall information about
the immediate past (E.g. Jack
recalls what he had for morning
snack when his aunt asks him
after lunch.)

9DDDE0278CA145C4A4699CE6260D6A08.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Demonstrate some
understanding of when things
happen in relation to routines

C64A592ECDC34BDF8C5A67E9DEF05AFB.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Associate a specific
occurrence with meeting their
needs (E.g. Emma hears
footsteps and lifts her arms
anticipating that mommy is
coming to pick her up.)

3C1FC61B2D1B4457B3339420C8AFD04C.description:
Concept of time
as it relates to
daily routines,
and sequencing
of events

475E383F195140469FCC918243F1F046.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Organize and represent information visually, with adult support (E.g. The teacher
helps the preschoolers create a picture graph showing the numbers of children
who walked to school or rode in a car.)

9022FA303DA54FBDAE9608150C436418.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Sort objects and count and compare the groups formed (E.g. Carlo says, “There
are 3 brown teddy bears and 4 black teddy bears.”

350182FBBC1B4775920A2BCCD5D1208D.description:
Three Years: Sort objects or people into
subgroups by one attribute

19A9C2636CB94F328F406665B4C24935.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Notice that objects can be
classified in different ways
based on different attributes
(E.g. Leo and Peter argue over
whether to sort their vehicles by
color or by size.)

56639C69F9C04D21AE5A9882CACA2A1F.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Can find people and objects
that are the same based on one
attribute

616F08DF5A974F1DB60D7F1D90797FCA.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can sort objects that are the
same and different on one
attribute (E.g. Amy puts all the
red vehicles in one basket.)

920A53B67173414FA9D9A2B2FE4897BA.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Focus on details in people and
objects in their environment

ECEB948A699543E4B4D3866CF5AB7997.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Focus attention to people or
objects in their environment
for a period of time

08F3C2E08A2044AD8E63EEE0A6458DE0.description:
Gathering,
organizing,
and analyzing
information,
and drawing
conclusions to
make sense of
the world

81271F2978C44D4E8018333F152A4CFC.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin creating simple patterns with familiar objects (E.g. Max places the blocks
in rows of long, short, long, short, etc.)

F9D61FE2CC574497BC28FFCA846A8AA6.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Order or sequence several objects based on one characteristic

DB416579DB3C482B8B4E611B29390E21.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Recognize simple patterns
(E.g. Malik looks at the plastic
animals on the shelf and says,
“Mommy, baby, mommy, baby.”)

5691894A3EBA45C88CFCB39BB77EABA8.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show awareness of and interest
in patterns

781C9202CF6745F197B0AC1359A599D0.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Show awareness of objects and
pictures that are the same

EDE1D4C160CB485CB1DA933665555546.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Explore similarities and
differences among objects in
their environment

200EB0D1DF434330BED028F0FC323D53.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Engage in sustained gazing
at objects or people, or track
movement with their eyes

96102C5106F04B0E94EFE12CAFA7A9B8.description:
Recognizing or
creating planned
or random
repetitions and
comparisons

8FF9AF4F8AD74C8D916A33DEBB25D96F.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Recognize that time is measured in units (E.g. John asks how many more
minutes he can stay outside.)

E49366465439446A80BC26CBD9176D83.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Make comparison such as bigger or smaller between two groups of objects

22FC875C795C42B98D7AEA06CA69B544.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Recognize that objects can be measured by height, length, weight, and volume
(E.g. Palo makes a stack of unifix cubes next to his friend and says, “You’re 40
cubes tall.”)

1DBCB1CE61BB4B00AFFC4174BE945BBC.description:
Three Years: Use non-standard tools
to measure, with adult
assistance (E.g. Marla, Stacy,
and Tim pass a lump of clay
between them to see if it is
bigger or smaller than each
child’s hand.)

1DC3AD91FE3D487AB435BC8B1460E32B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Recognize that objects and
people can be measured
(E.g. Brianna asks her mother,
“How big am I?”)

6B57E485D8894963BA4B0A1C1E54C23F.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show awareness of measurable
qualities, such as size, distance,
temperature, and weight, which,
in toddler terms, are big/small,
near/far, hot/cold, heavy/light

AFDADD8086374AAE95F2A7A771A304ED.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Explore the concept of volume
(E.g. Chase and Jade pick up a
bucket of sand and dump it into
the sandbox, over and over.)

4AAE5D3430EE42F7A851DA4C6DA29DA3.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show some awareness of the
relative size of objects in their
environment

DBECD3E7FCB04F478BD57FF813006A38.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Explore and begin to notice
differences in temperature of
objects in their environment

423FB01D43334641B3C4E2C2033070B8.description:
Size, volume,
quantity, and
other measurable
qualities, and the
tools to measure
them

29EF84C1D5474E98BDAF307953B04EFA.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Compare the shape of two objects (E.g. Reanna draws two round shapes and
says, “This one is an oval and this one is a circle.”)

DC8BFBA1B9EB4DD7B08205B96AB4B830.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Describes basic features of shapes (E.g. Finnley says, “This triangle has three
sides and this square has four sides.”)

8BAB30A966964202877FBF5F9F2EB8A3.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Identify and name common shapes

912D7B3303924F7F9823B086704A7038.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use words that show understanding of order and position of objects

0160D6DB5D094C34A9DB750211013D90.description:
Three Years: Explore and identify shapes in
their environment and begin to
notice attributes of shapes with
adult help (E.g. Addy, 3 years
old, says, “Look, my paper
plate is a circle!”)

1F4767298AB34FDD8E29A46DDA2AAAD3.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Use comparison words and
position words correctly

7318CD7BEAC243E89198E30CCCAB9366.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Demonstrate an understanding
of many position words
(E.g. Brittany says to her
teacher, “I’m next to you.”)

E20CC6D7FEB847FF9F22A72F3782C169.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Demonstrate an understanding
of simple position words
(E.g. Hayden climbs a hill and
says, “Me on top!”)

525EDC7CE78740E9BD6209AA885644E4.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Demonstrate an awareness
of the distance between their
body and materials in space
(E.g. Jayce crawls across the
room to grab a toy.)

2F28018FAF224DECBBC0028062DF56BB.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Develop an understanding
of where things are in their
environment

E40AD3D4D6B74506B7ED4E03C434A84E.description:
Shapes and
their attributes,
position,
comparing and
contrasting two or
more objects, and
distance

0D713A4696CC4756AB33B8AB3625D238.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to recognize and attempt to write numerals up to 10

E2A17E3DEDC549CC8A5913EBBE8CED17.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: *While many children move through all of the steps of this sequence by five years
old, others may still be only partially through this sequence by that age.

31B421FDA1DF45988FF95EB4D656E1F3.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Change small collections of objects by combining or removing objects and then
counting to determine how many they have (E.g. Avery counts out three blocks,
then adds two more, and counts all of the blocks and says, “I have five blocks.”)

C2A360C821CE4DC592F6CEF6768DFE7E.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Can answer the question “What comes after...” a number without having to
recount (E.g. When asked, “What comes after five,” Sawyer says, “Six,” without
having to count up from one.)

0DCE47595ED840E69F674C1EF67181FB.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Count objects in two different collections (up to ten in each) to determine which
is the larger one

592CBA57B12A431B91D357588C9B73FF.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Recognize that the last number used in counting is the same as the total
(E.g. Leila counts four cars and when the teacher asks her, “How many cars do
you have?” she answers, “Four.”)

098AD6E2DF95447F8FE0AB7B4897353B.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Demonstrate understanding of one-to-one correspondence

833C71B2AF5F4F08B87667492BE4B68B.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Identify by sight how many are in a small group of up to 3 items

6B9F9090CFE640359793AA9467E012AB.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Develop progressively more complex knowledge and skills about numbers, in the
following sequence*:

7793B4C934E24AD18E76B656F53D3CC9.description:
Three Years: Show an interest in counting
1 to 10, may hold up fingers
to indicate quantity

84916058A9184A4EB7DC88A0C8D421AD.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Begin to initiate one-to-one
matching for four or fewer
items

E8C762C6E171450983634D43D28E65C9.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Develop an understanding
of the relationship between
spoken numbers and quantity
for quantities up to 2 or 3
(E.g. Blake picks up a car and
a block and says, “Two toys.”)

089EF4C7B6F54940BB8B2794700A220C.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can use number words in
songs and finger plays without
understanding that numbers
represent quantity

43D5BF1830DE42EBA7DA6AAC1ADA8F13.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Begin to understand the
concepts of “more” and “all
gone” and begin to request
“more” or indicate “no more”
verbally or non-verbally

603CA8F0C8F2465080C04A8C8D2D000F.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Develop an awareness of
one or more than one
(E.g. 7-month-old Gary holds
one toy in one hand, another
toy in the other hand.)

061D51AB1D794A2AB0E1541F05B05FF1.description:
Concept
of number,
quantity, ways
of representing
numbers,
one-to-one
correspondence,
and counting

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

9949791EA35144A89CD50313020E760E.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Show interest in issues of friendship and fairness

895C91D239994038B7B2BF643BB1B3DD.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Act out family roles and occupations in dramatic play

DA9BBD2156854AE39F68E90A3BE20BE2.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Recognize some people, places, and occupations in their communities

6B4ECF28210347E7801A325F7F1DE376.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Notice similarities and differences in people, families, and social groups

9552885F22864C979B4DDFAF2885A7C6.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Are aware of own family relationships and show curiosity about others’ families

8B6E9240F6534F049B521ACE7F939B01.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Know basic personal information

64C34ADE284B4C61B2BDEFBBA4807208.description:
Three Years: Ask questions about other
people’s experiences in their
families and communities

677D30E63CA2408B8F247FC48694166B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Explore various roles in
their home and classroom
(E.g. Natalie tells James, 20
months old, that he is the baby
and that she is going to be
the mommy. She then begins
acting out the role by giving
him a bottle.)

1F61CAF3133D4054AD63805D5353B7FA.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May sort items or toys into
“families” and label with
different roles in their own terms

4BFC2D9CF825445A803743F55A5D2A44.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Identify family members of other
children in their class

9A11E5916E7640AABF4E7EEBA2D5EA17.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Interact with members of their
household and their classroom
Relates to social/emotional
construct of relationships and
social skills with peers

C8C80E82C29D4E7E9D311E101813E4BE.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Recognize primary caregivers

2635D25E5DC2453695762C252911D85F.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: With guidance from adults, can engage in problem-solving to resolve difference
in perspectives

4951697716554898BBEDC3B5983C6561.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Practice culturally appropriate social conventions (E.g. Satori uses chopsticks
when eating meals at home.)

EDD7A88D40E84DFB934ADFD2E73EC2F5.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Participate in developing classroom rules

82D6117129B44BE48FB7F3962C2BBD34.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Show interest in caring for the classroom environment

4C9E248116D344F9BCF106F2000E5098.description:
Three Years: Demonstrate and follow
different customs in different
settings

FF8BC18ACC7B45AA951513C9CD502673.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Understand that certain rules
and customs apply in some
situations and not in others
(E.g. Sam tells his baby sister,
“No yelling in church.”)

82CA7782B811476AB97FADCB7E9726DF.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Participate in expected behavior
including greetings and goodbyes

0F709448A9DA461BA071AF438514ECE1.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Recognize that there are
routines and may test the
expectations

040DFA82C6DB4E35927E937A913C9A15.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Use culturally appropriate labels
for people and relationships in
their family

F1DBED39E43440DDBE81A1F48E188262.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Recognize cultural and
social labels for people and
relationships in their family

1FE602C3A84A48D299CFA9847F119EA7.description:
Explore simple physical science concepts such as force, motion, and gravity
(E.g. Three children in the preschool room build an elaborate structure with blocks
and ramps and then run different marbles through it to see which is the fastest.)

D98FCDAA7B71482DBAF70997A83545C9.description: Show interest in caring for the earth and environment

A67FF6216D9942EF9F129E74554A538E.description:
Begin to talk about environmental changes and phenomena (weather, seasons,
sun, and moon)

E102793B981B40DC9C2F9055F2915148.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to identify the properties of various living things and what living things
need to be able to survive

BE9942B8DBB844738DBD422BBB66EF7E.description:
Three Years: Ask many questions about the
physical world and investigate
with adult guidance

4CD06DBB7ADE4DF1BDDE12838648F382.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Focus on small details in indoor
and outdoor environment
(E.g. Esme lays on the grass
and watches an ant move.)

600BC966C0EC4F34BC71FEB3A1E13F3E.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show interest in observing,
experiencing, and/or exploring
physical science concepts and
the natural world

FB6B785422334A9180C68FC812DB7CD0.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Through repeated observation,
experimentation, and/or
exploration, further develop their
understanding of basic physical
science concepts and the
natural world

0DA3445DA8E740389D17A8A933B1BA02.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Through trial and error, begin
to develop an understanding
of some basic physical science
concepts such as gravity, force,
and motion. (E.g. Penelope
repeatedly drops her cup off the
high chair and watches it fall to
the floor.)

105C4C674A644804875CC924A058F8BC.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Explore objects in various ways
using their senses

5B0B364C42D3494383DDE1B4A1D9443C.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use a variety of forms (drawings, block structures, movement, and other
materials) to represent their ideas and feelings

FB3D5A6AEDAB46B8959CA2EF82FBAF5B.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Talk about things or people that are not present

2F4076EEA9694B899D5AB2CB4E8C9110.description: Three Years: Play simple memory games

0D53BC4D49E54092954B5171E8C7EDE7.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Enjoy hiding games

577CBB1A80614AEBBC24DFB851CB40CD.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Ask for people or things that are
not in sight

FF2EE40EE9CE446CA76C71ECC3A592C6.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can find objects that are not in
sight

8D00D69C04AA410DA62700E395968AD7.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show understanding that people
and objects no longer in sight
still exist (E.g. Molly watches
her mother put keys in her
purse. Molly then searches in
the purse to find them.)

9CBFEE92948D4542BB642C56DEE87D1E.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Track moving objects and
begin to understand that
people and objects no longer
in sight still exist

standardSets.title: Cognitive Development – Approaches to Learning: Birth-5
standardSets.subject: Early Learning Standards (2016-)

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

943862BE2D734A08A15D30A2446F7FDA.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Understand that symbols on pictographs and bar graphs indicate quantity
(E.g. Chethan puts a sticker on the class graph to show that he has a cat at
home and remarks, “More children have a dog at home than a cat.”)

3B1AAE75906F4D559B8EE66407C50DBF.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Use objects to represent other objects in their pretend play (E.g. Hadley and
Kayla build an elaborate castle using couch cushions and blankets.)

EF86ED4D0CA04B80B0B0BD77155A244D.description:
Three Years: Are aware that some symbols
represent words and numbers

F4EB0BC50E714A86A83F7CFF9E807D6C.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Understand that some signs
in the community represent
familiar places

AD0C69155BC84B23A05C761F3E21E567.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use a variety of materials,
media, and other forms of selfexpression to represent their
thinking (E.g. Tessa makes up
songs about herself.)

48E74EF99589441EBDE9637AFC3D7F47.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Use an object to represent
something else

37A694F5CE184FF0BE0F2769C2D2B7CC.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May draw comfort from objects
that represent family members
or primary caregivers (E.g. Bertti
keeps her mother’s scarf in her
cubby and clings to it when
upset.)

2F3EE673D0634A1296D4E1493B9A5423.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Calm in the presence of
their primary caregiver
(E.g. Gigi clings to her teacher
when a stranger enters the
classroom.)

65C1412BB6244D23BC1D71C6152176E9.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: May get frustrated if they cannot carry out their goals to the level of mastery
they desire

D5C5F59CA676489D9CFE43D403341353.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Take the initiative carrying out their own plans and persist until the goal is
achieved

E6011F9BA3854D6A954492F7ACF0906C.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Demonstrate a desire to please adults and may seek adult attention
(E.g. 4-year-old Zara yells “Watch me! Watch me!” as she walks across the
balance beam.)

D24E70968918491D80EA4597FA784A07.description:
Three Years: Show initiative in a variety of
ways including offering to help

4B0372A2AFA74FFC97562556347BA271.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Demonstrate the motivation to
master simple tasks

9D2EA5F1680145268D7D01E167B1B336.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Persist in following their own
curiosity even if adults try to
deter them (E.g. 24-month-old
Sebastian keeps dropping his
toy cars in the toilet bowl even
though his mother tells him
not to.)

E9AFC8A233FF45BA9FD61C25EA6F5706.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Initiate simple plans
(E.g. 20-month-old Abreeanna
pulls on her teacher’s hand
and says, “out”, as she walks
to the door.)

0760C4E3198042809EE0F31ABEBEDC70.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Explore objects that interest
them with focus and persistence

EA69BC14E2DA4D44B4274F4D670B6237.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Persist in pursuing objects
of interest (E.g. 9-monthold Jasper crawls after her
family’s cat.)

3150701C986F4F6CA9BAC529A2E60E47.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Stay focused for longer periods of time on activities that interest them and
return to those activities

AD3302C75BCB43A3B44CAE729C005933.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Keep track of more than one thing at a time

7B4A9D303C914AD89063ABD1108435D1.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Pay attention to and remember details

142DB089BD4642CA8A92D478A866A40A.description:
Three Years: Can play simple memory
games such as matching
pictures on cards

F2F66EBF76174D4ABEC5D1415DF0DB29.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Can maintain attention on their
choice of activity until they have
achieved their goal (E.g. Cheng
draws one more line on her
picture and says, “All done.”)

B6F661847FA24840AF5586860E26E9A0.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Have increased attention spans
for activities that interest them
or that they initiate

583C21A5D85E448C813A1E2012CD5D37.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Stay focused on simple stories
or books for brief periods of time

DA9183E8D7DD4A1B8DAFCCDEB4CFE927.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Can have expectations of what
will happen based on previous
experiences (E.g. Wilfred pulls
his mother’s hand to bring her
to the refrigerator knowing she
will offer juice to him.)

A96E181B2F3E43B5991AD4CDBBF6E3C1.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Begin to maintain focus
despite distractions during
brief delays

3BF1AB3AA147475C94CD8A8A03F40238.description:
Working memory
and focus and
attention

61567ACE327248FB9CBA54A1ACA72829.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: May ask for help on own or with teacher prompting or seek more information
when needed

7240A3165B5A42AF960D4FE2BEE40D7D.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Can engage in increasingly complex planning (E.g. The 4-year-olds create very
complex rules for the game they are playing on the playground.)

C2FD6557011C41898E813EEB3720BB89.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Can adapt their plan to include other children with adult guidance

4E0095B50924481D861D48A0F483F4AA.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to show ability to adapt their plans when they can’t follow through with
their original idea

5D7A6A3B7C934299BC931CE91225FED1.description:
Three Years: Can adapt plans to
incorporate new materials

E510AABCD0EC49AE91E803F25EFFB51F.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Plan their own simple activities
and organize the materials
they need

924BA511A6A24BF0A52F46FF52D442A5.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Can try to figure out what is
getting in the way of their plan

54D11598B6B04FC6B1857D56D1FF3D51.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Plan and implement a two-step
dramatic play (E.g. Ezra pretends
to feed the baby doll and then
puts it in the baby bed.)

A81ADB28AA204EE1B15B7F9686076747.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Can carry out their own onestep plan (E.g. Penthia puts a
hat on her head.)

8253D805D8794E368F0D34E2C479FEDA.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Can act intentionally to
achieve a goal (E.g. 8-monthold Oscar rolls across the floor
to reach a toy.)

B0D5756646134866A1EDE20C898BAC9A.description:
Adaptability
of thought
processes,
planning, and
intentionality

A82B32A0F17C48228B70BB01F92D0DEF.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Pretend to be characters from stories, books, television shows, movies, or their
own invention

62B472D6D4A54A2C9B695C17C70001C9.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Create games that continue to evolve as they plan

D079892DF1EB470BAC68782C81306ECC.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Tell elaborate stories of their own invention or add details to stories

251C086C59614F988052159A60A94261.description:
Three Years: Laugh at themselves when
they do something silly

CE807E96284E41BBAEDB3816C1986B11.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Play exuberantly

FE451E7FAE8D485B83C191752726844B.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Are amused by incongruity
(E.g. Jonah laughs hysterically
when his father pretends to put
Jonah’s shoes on his big feet.)

280E53D9465644A49162D99F0702C970.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Take delight in repetitive games
and interactions (E.g. Bodhi and
his teacher pass a ball back and
forth and each time the teacher
pretends to stop, Bodhi says,
“again” and laughs when the
teacher starts again.)

F9AA682E8ADB4BE5BE37F005CFB18864.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Express delight in ways
appropriate to their culture

E96116CCE821418D8279A78430CF16C9.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Show pleasure in simple
sensory games (E.g. AJ’s
mother tugs at the blanket in
his hands and he tugs it back
toward himself. They do this
several times as AJ laughs.)

232C2D474A324778A38A93A5F956DF6D.description:
Sense of delight
and humor*
*delight and humor are
culturally influenced

36EB15984493482ABACAD13779FD563A.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: May share physical humor with one another

3FBCDCE2B45141CE840659EE58407933.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Begin to understand simple jokes

803D884289FD47C9ABE520FC76FA022C.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: May play with language including “bathroom” words

12C81A4A9F2740508AB38E3C35CB076E.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Show delight in all aspects of play from planning to describing the experience

8F5874CE6DCA41F194F5DA29784AFAB8.description: Three Years: Invent stories and characters

FD224BC006524B6A968137AB7892543D.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Engage in more extended
pretend play

DFAB28B7DE18476DAAB22679084CA593.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Begin to engage in simple
pretend games

5E350BDDD6E34D7B9BD5080762D066EC.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Play with toys in ways of their
own invention. (E.g. Kai puts
blocks and cars together in a
single structure.)

96EA1A1CF2354AA991002BBA0E41C994.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May invent ways to attract adult
attention and engage with them
(E.g. Gretta pretends to cough
to gain her teacher’s attention
and repeats this when her
teacher laughs.)

E0BB99D82165489DA7EDB0911FBAE8F8.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Infants this young do not
demonstrate creativity,
imagination, and inventiveness
in ways that adults can easily
interpret

99F1910EA88F44C8BA40FE5432B2CF93.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Create sophisticated structures alone and with others, using various constructive
materials, sometimes used in pretend play

6C75B94A818D49D8AFA5CFA59C12926F.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Engage in pretend play with others to explore and understand life experience
and roles

9E5BFFAB180449AF868D747719699430.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Co-create elaborate pretend play with other children, including scenarios with
multiple roles, ideas, and co-negotiated rules

A696ED44EAB94159B99E01EAC9CC861A.description:
Three Years: Engage in pretend play
that includes roles and
experiences that they find
challenging (E.g. After a visit
to the doctor, Brett gives her
doll a shot.)

8528BD24D7AA41F0BAAF8B4D7063D169.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Take risks in big body play,
expanding their physical abilities

00F19F07A9E34BD290BF83E3033B8434.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Try out new actions, roles, and
words that they imitate from
others

F18928E041F74725BFA180A7992ECE55.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Enjoy using their whole bodies in
active play

0142AAD416494EF9A9CB5D532C7E336A.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May initiate turn taking with
a trusted adult (E.g. Spencer
gives a small toy to his
grandmother and she gives
another toy to him. They repeat
this several times.)

E8B087F6B91444B7883048FD2EDA3BCC.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Engage in turn taking
interactions with adults and
explore a variety of materials
including their own bodies,
people, and objects

E3184CD51F5A4995952157F5E8011A1A.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Work with others to plan or problem solve toward a shared goal and can describe
the reasons for their shared decisions (E.g. Aaron, Chuck, and Jill make a
complex track for a train and discuss how sharp curves make trains derail.)

CAB232A734344D6EB8041827F2C2A57C.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Can figure out more than one solution to a problem if the first one doesn’t work
(E.g. In trying to get a ball down from the tree, Marlow first throws a shoe to
get it down and when that doesn’t work, gets a rake to try to poke it down.)

CCF48DBAE10345F1B2354BF05684418C.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Talk about own ideas, predictions, and plans, building on prior experiences
either self-initiated or guided by adults

5E2E4F24E69C46A1BC3E9EC171DE55E1.description:
Three Years: Remember strategies that
have worked and apply them
to new situations (E.g. At
home, Davis moves a stool
to the sink so that he can
reach for his toothbrush. At
child care the next day, Davis
struggles to reach a pencil on
the counter so he picks up
a chair and puts it near the
counter.)

753B492053F24101A1C557F412E91831.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Solve some problems without
having to physically try out all
possible solutions and may ask
for help when needed

25D7BAFE76E54895BD0B4BAE4AD5CDEC.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use multiple strategies to solve
simple problems, but may
become frustrated when their
strategies don’t work

1D3C930ACE9C421FBA506B487E120DF6.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Process and assimilate new
information and experiences
by comparing them to previous
information and experiences to
expand their understanding of
the world (E.g. Margaret sees a
horse for the first time and says,
“Big doggie!”)

617C943DFB7C46AC808ACD5FCD9CFC7E.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Act out ideas about how things
work by repeating and changing
their actions (trial and error)

D93F231015CB4484BF4115B13E55E97E.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Seek to make sense of what
happens in their environment

D50827A1CDA14307B775740950164740.description:
Theories about
the world and how
things work
(Reflection,
critical thinking,
and trial and
error)

C05B77ED2F774153B1EFBC6C7F0E9138.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Engage in repeated actions to make something happen (E.g. Dannie notices
that Marie buttons her own coat, so Dannie tries several methods before
succeeding in buttoning her own coat.)

0E04DA2404E848F4995031B4852D4B05.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Continue to experiment with cause and effect

6C7C3930D8BC4298BAD67515994A97C3.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Sometimes use magical thinking, showing misunderstanding of cause and effect
(E.g. Zeke puts his snow pants by the front door, believing that this will make it
snow overnight.)

FA52EB34A6E440FD9F3B51AF720DF514.description:
Three Years: Use variations on previous
actions in new environments
and with different objects to
create new and desired effects

F0D855582A0D4E0EAD5C215D9B19C713.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Anticipate and try to prevent
another person’s actions that
will create undesirable effects

613FEDA6BB88430BA450B072699EDCCD.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Repeat actions to create the
same effect and add variations
of those actions to see if the
same thing happens

8AEEB12EBE03404F8AD092D0E86626E4.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Experiment with cause and
effect while investigating their
environment

0EFA0351CEA245ADB54E6668F8C5E4E9.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May do things to get a response
from familiar adults and children
(E.g. Luke drops peas and looks
over to his caregiver as they fall
from the table to the floor.)

8A2E375B794B460E8A0F6632A4641F9B.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Understand that their actions
can have an effect on
people and objects in their
environment and repeat
actions to duplicate effects
(E.g. Colleen gently bounces
6-month-old Rory on her
lap. When she stops, Rory
moves his body up and down
until Colleen resumes the
bouncing.)

68C0EF6D3FE142669A920B77FE23B714.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use senses and tools/technology to aid in investigation

21736490E2AD45D28435BE1AB15EEC64.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Observe, wonder, and/or ask questions, make guesses, and explore hypotheses

D3CA58ADE3A1483E9E528796726A6257.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Continue to seek information
through observation,
exploration, and asking
questions

2353D2CAF64D4A0BA01616ECF6EBD47D.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Seek information through
observation, exploration, and
use of simple tools (E.g. Arthur
pulls a chair up to the kitchen
counter to see what his father is
making for dinner.)

A26C431F0139466EB3454BEADA776C1F.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Continue to investigate people
and objects as tools

69AF980AA1254EA28346986BCF396939.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Explore objects using their
senses and manipulate them in
a variety of ways

EB3BD5E600A44C15A7C0A156750FAC55.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Show awareness of
occurrences in their
surroundings and use their
senses to explore people and
objects

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

E19C3969F3944D579B82C2709C54ACAB.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Demonstrate increasing independence with basic health care skills, if culturally
appropriate (E.g. 4-year-old Saygan blows his nose using a tissue and then
goes to the sink to wash his hands with soap and water.)

89DF82E2A9B9492B99B4D8BC9910CB69.description:
Three Years: Seek to accomplish self-care
and house-keeping tasks
with reminders, if culturally
appropriate

51E7224B2E344F709162A5D897DDAE6E.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Are more likely to willingly
participate in self-care routines,
if culturally appropriate

719FF75653E34B5CA19D7B51A236AAA3.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Are able to participate in and
occasionally initiate simple
health routines, if culturally
appropriate

56C7390003A34433B4ECCE8136F09EF7.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Show increasing interest in
and sometimes insistence on
doing things for themselves, if
culturally appropriate (E.g. Preda
insists on putting the soap on
her hands without help.)

92F7EBE9F3974642B59C95BD1796A062.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: May be able to participate,
with adult assistance, in selfcare tasks such as dressing
and undressing, and feeding
themselves, if culturally
appropriate

BAFDAA6D7D2040E28F688331A9C04218.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Note: Infants at this age rely
on adults to care for them
(E.g. Joey washes 8-monthold Dana’s hands after a
diaper change.)

FD8C975EE06C4F5AB236369D6BB062D5.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Follow basic health and safety rules with some reminders and/or guidance from
adults (E.g. 5-year-old Miles stops at the curb while on a walk with his mother.
He looks both ways, holds his mom’s hand, and then crosses the street at the
crosswalk.)

974A6E8F62F04A969AED19BE032F529E.description:
Three Years: Can identify and explain
familiar health and safety
signs in the community

F7232DAD258E4B3F872EECC0B5733D8B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Show increasing awareness of
health and safety practices

6C12A72295954D228ECDA1D55FDB92F5.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May acknowledge potentially
unsafe situations, but are not
yet able to be responsible for
their own safety (E.g. Felipe
climbs to the top of the toddler
loft but needs a teacher’s
assistance to get down.)

323DA3AF7E1F47779FFE78D0D2BA8923.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Look to primary caregivers when
faced with new or unfamiliar
people or environments
Relates to social/emotional
construct of relationships with
unfamiliar adults

BC105501CEF642DCB9F480576FE95347.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Seek physical contact with
primary caregivers when faced
with new or unfamiliar people or
environments
Relates to social/emotional
construct of relationships with
primary caregivers

85521D4C93134BB4B54250A481FA0FFC.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Cry to indicate stress and to
seek help

D193FC2FC8CF4251B4675E399953EFFD.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: When asked, are able to name nutritious alternatives

D99F8FBBAAF94D9DA623EF08C1A218F1.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Recognize and eat a variety of nutritious foods

ACD2C438F6D94C888267CA2EC1A3691E.description:
Three Years: Try healthy foods from a
variety of cultures when given
the opportunity

7464ED759246413794FD1F671858890F.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Show some awareness that
some foods are more nutritious
than others (E.g. After Brian
reads We Eat Food That’s
Fresh, Kara points to the fresh
strawberries on her plate at
snack time.)

A5A7A3052EB94202A06195A772EEF87C.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Demonstrate a willingness to try
new foods if offered on multiple
occasions

17B6ED8E452542218EEFD134D4140BD8.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Successfully chew and bite
foods of varying textures

889A33922D744C42813DD46B1312C96C.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Chew and bite and develop the
ability to eat finger foods

34763D9C0C114B908E38B1DF54CC411E.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Suck and swallow liquids and
associate breast or bottle with
being fed

52ACC7A0DAA1425C8EB8E268E79E2AD7.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Demonstrate greater dexterity with a variety of tools such as eating utensils,
crayons, keyboards, paint brushes, and scissors

F7859700DB3B455086FF0E312A3B99F7.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Continue to develop small muscle control and coordination (E.g. 4-year-old
Emily uses her index finger and her thumb to form the clay into animal like
shapes.)

3A3C3A6554DB44F29FD97338EACCE464.description:
Three Years: Show increased confidence
in ability to coordinate small
muscles and interest in new
ways to use small muscles

C72F56710E5A4BBB8E5CF1F9B29AB041.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Use smaller manipulatives with
ease

224E46049D514938A8E18F7348E23CF0.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use tools purposefully to
accomplish a goal (E.g. Shelby
uses a glue stick to glue paper
onto a wall collage.)

9FD77311B2C941F5AE75FDCA7492061C.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Reach, grasp, and release
objects with more control and
experiment with using tools

ED135DCA6F1349429C9E770CBA1FF961.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Coordinate eyes and hands while
exploring or holding objects

CA5E6F28886347539EDB7390731EC7BB.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Move from awareness of
hands to ability to reach and
grasp objects of varying sizes

918011BB243B4EEAA6CE96F268BDF553.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Use a variety of materials and equipment in gross motor activities

88CAA645EE854F1F8FE77C179839D1C0.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds:  Increase their strength, balance, flexibility, and stamina

F4D215C2687A494BBD10B8254D7E99A7.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Continue to develop large muscle control and coordination to play more complex
games and/or perform more controlled actions (E.g. Juanita, 5 years old, tosses
a stone on the hopscotch game, hops on one foot through two squares and
then jumps on two feet to complete the game.)

A2BA4F64C3DA49B48ED29FDA123E07A1.description:
Three Years: Show increased confidence in
their ability to coordinate large
muscles and interest in new
ways to use large muscles

A37A1F7D248B413EA880B3D944AAF139.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Purposefully explore with their
whole body and use objects
and equipment

2AB67D8216E14874BEB510383EF5793F.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Have more control with their
arm and leg movements for
walking, running, climbing, etc.

3539DA515F684B1A87E5D443AA321329.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Move from one place to another
by walking and running with
basic control and coordination

C44119E8310F471C921BD0608390A3E6.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Become mobile, progressing
from crawling to walking, and
show strong interest in climbing

7098B29524814FBAAB20E81FD637207D.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Develop head and trunk stability
and ability to change positions

3A9588A9E15D40A682F90606E05C6356.description:
Three Years: May be able to identify the
need to eliminate

77443830300A4FFA9E4879D23D7B32C9.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: May take initiative to make
themselves more comfortable
(E.g. Remey takes off his socks
and says, “Too hot.”)

154D40F15B374F94876D15D261DB3F30.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May resist sleeping or napping
even when tired

956AF608280F48FC856B1D19BC2CF25A.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can show tiredness or hunger
through predictable behaviors

7E7F9F92D2F64E7B9F6FBEA498EADF61.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: By the end of this age range are
eating three meals per day plus
snacks

5C8C910167734105A1921172700EAD63.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Begin to develop predictable
patterns for sleeping, eating,
and eliminating

B6FB1FA3426B4A9EBE439A02F7866589.description:
Three Years: Develop the ability to use one
sense to predict what they
would perceive with another
(E.g. Jowanna reaches into the
mystery bag and guesses that
she is holding a teddy bear
based on the way it feels.)

92A3453974904FB9B240495DB9D6575B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Begin to focus on important
stimuli while ignoring
extraneous stimuli

EE041F463EA740838DA40D7BA347062A.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Use the information received
from their senses to change
the way they interact with the
environment

D8006DC6DA0E4EBEB27F42A407BA83B7.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Demonstrate sensory
preferences (E.g. After playing
in the sand in the sensory table,
Anne wipes her hands together
and leaves when the teacher
adds water to make mud.)

3BFDE875479946D4A63351A08233B72B.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Use senses to experience
objects and the environment

9D96AD93991E4B5DAFABF503D016E4AD.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Show awareness of and
respond to sensory stimuli

2420584A3393483A992E6960F678E10B.description:
Development
of the senses,
orientation
to stimuli,
and sensory
integration

7B011F45F93B4222A0B137EEBD8B0FF1.description: Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Increasingly use eye-hand coordination to perform a variety of tasks

00607037CA794CE996BA8D936EC04496.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Continue to develop their ability to move their body in space and control their
bodily movements (E.g. Tanya maneuvers her wheelchair up a ramp and around
a corner to join her friends.)

D89D445C60C64DD88539B4163F8ADB61.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Participate in a variety of physical activities to enhance personal health and
physical fitness

4F6D6A449AD24F68BD2217E01235516E.description:
Three Years: Move with confidence
and stability, coordinating
movements to accomplish
simple tasks (E.g. Outside on
the playground, a small group
of children play a game of
Duck, Duck, Goose.)

25A050647BEB46C18E40F99F09EE5921.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Move their bodies through
space with balance and control

AFAC3020D3884B04B2E2B4E849BE68AB.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show increased balance and
coordination in play activities

46522920B27440ADBA65F4D69FD8DD05.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Can negotiate moving around
objects and people without
bumping into them

4FB653840B8646B6A113AB8CB649F0E9.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Become more aware of where
their body is in relation to
other objects and people in the
environment

8FCE0DFF9D744842887B3EC7B52D809E.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Use many repetitions to
move various body parts and
gain increasing control over
movements

standardSets.title: Creative Expression and Aesthetic Appreciation: Birth-5
standardSets.subject: Early Learning Standards (2016-)

document.title: NH-Early-Learning-Standards

81ACCCF3712D4FB88746D04E6100E4B6.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Show interest and respect for the creative work of self and others, and share
experiences and ideas about art and creative expression

B38F7A9C9FEF47C3821CBC2D0ABBC71D.description:
Three Years: Use descriptive words to
express their response to
an aesthetic experience
(E.g. Using his communication
device, Mark tells Tory he
really likes the colors in her
painting.)

870BBFB206F54FAA88212C60C7ABD14B.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Exclaim enthusiastically in
response to experiencing
beauty indoors or outdoors
(E.g. Ginny and her friends
jump up and down shouting,
“It’s a rainbow,” when they see
a rainbow in the sprinkler.)

3FC42EBAD7AB4BF9A838A287B4C359BD.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: May participate actively in
singing songs and dancing

9735D5C1E135430ABDEEDCE125FE9A49.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Express joy in aesthetic
experience

F5D369A5EBC1405BA15B96226D84DC89.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Respond with delight to some
experiences, environments, and
specific sensations

5297AD64FDBE4093A40F468CBCC38220.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Enjoy and respond to sights,
sounds, textures, tastes, and
smells

2B32483929FA4BB9ABF90A72B2EE7EA0.description:
Four- and Five-Year-Olds: Discuss and evaluate the music, art, drama, dance, and natural phenomena
they have witnessed

025EF06221414933814DDFB56DCEC9F8.description:
Three Years: Share opinions about likes
and dislikes in art and
creative expression

9040FEB3F88F4A04ABE3BAF0AD2792BC.description:
Thirty Months to
Three Years: Try to reproduce aspects of
music, art, drama, dance, and
natural phenomena they have
witnessed (E.g. After watching
a tap dancer, Reagan, Andrew,
and Gabe recreate tap dancing.)

D288BA94C486421785B36426E3247991.description:
Twenty-Four to
Thirty Months: Show what they notice about
the music, art, drama, dance,
and natural phenomena they
have witnessed

2DBDCA6D712E44AEB6491230F32D235C.description:
Eighteen to
Twenty-Four Months: Begin to focus on and
distinguish details in the indoor
and outdoor environments

6CC8915946B341B8BAA16DC25666ED3C.description:
Nine Months to
Eighteen Months
: Show awareness of and
preference for specific textures,
smells, sounds, and visual
images (E.g. Kathryn uses
her hands to pick up a piece
of birthday cake and then
repeatedly wipes her hands on
her shirt saying, “No.”)

524F385F1F804E1D861DCE7E153E99BA.description:
Birth to
Nine Months: Focus on sounds, patterns,
and movements in the indoor
and outdoor environment
(E.g. Colin, 8 months old,
giggles when he feels the
breeze on his face.)
